title: Your Emergency Plan
intro: This part puts the plan on paper: who to call, where to meet, when and how you would leave, what the people and animals in your home need, and how warnings will reach you. Each list is a printable sheet that you fill in by hand and keep yourself. The last steps test the plan while nothing is wrong.
credit: Based on Unit 2 of Oregon's Be 2 Weeks Ready toolkit (Activities 6 to 9, pages 48 to 57), with additions for city and apartment households.

actions.title: List everyone in your household with a cell number
actions.why: You may need every name and number at once, and a phone with a flat battery cannot give them to you.
actions.how: Print the Household sheet. Write one row for each person who lives with you: full name and mobile number, and leave the other columns for later. Fill it in by hand and keep it yourself; this site only records that it is done.
actions.done: The Household sheet has a row for each person who lives with you, with a full name and a mobile number.

actions.title: Write down the services each person relies on
actions.why: The doctor, pharmacy, school and carer are the numbers you will need most and remember least.
actions.how: Print the Emergency numbers sheet. Fill in the doctor, pharmacy, school or childcare, workplace, landlord or building manager, and any home-care or equipment supplier: name, phone and one line of notes. Copy the numbers from your phone, bills and prescription labels. Write by hand and keep the sheet yourself; the site only records that you did it.
actions.done: The doctor, pharmacy and any home-care or equipment supplier for each person are on the printed numbers sheet.

actions.title: Write down your main insurance policies
actions.why: After a loss the first thing an insurer asks for is the policy number, and the paper it was printed on may be gone.
actions.how: Print the Insurance and legal list. For each policy you hold now (renters or home, health, car), write the company and its claims phone number, adding only the last four digits of the policy number if you need them to tell policies apart. You will find them on the first page of the policy, on your insurance card or in the insurer's app. Fill it in by hand and store it with your documents; this site only records that it is done.
actions.done: The Insurance and legal list shows the company and claims phone number for each policy you hold now, and it is stored with your documents.

actions.title: Write down who supplies your power, gas and water, and their outage numbers
actions.why: You cannot report an outage or a leak quickly if the number is on a website you cannot load.
actions.how: Print the Utilities list. From a recent bill, copy the provider and its outage or emergency phone number for electricity, gas and water. If the landlord pays for a service, write the building manager's after-hours number in that row instead. Fill it in by hand and keep it yourself; the site only records that you did it.
actions.done: The electricity, gas and water rows of the Utilities list each hold a provider's outage or emergency number, or the building manager's after-hours number.
actions.apartment: In many apartments the water, sewer and sometimes heat are in the building's name, so the number that matters most is management's after-hours line.

actions.title: List your banks and cards, lock the list away and tell one person where it is
actions.why: If your wallet or phone is lost you need to know which accounts exist and which number freezes a card, and the same list would help a thief, so where it is kept matters as much as what is on it.
actions.how: Print the Bank and bills list. For each bank, card, loan, pension and investment account, write the institution's name, the type of account, its website, the customer service or lost-card phone number, and only the last four digits of the account or card number. Never write passwords, PINs or full card numbers on it. Seal it in an envelope and keep it in a locked box with your documents, never on the fridge or as a photo on your phone. Tell one trusted person where it is.
actions.done: The Bank and bills list, with every bank, card and loan and no passwords, is sealed in an envelope in a locked box, and one trusted person has been told where it is.

actions.title: Choose two meeting places, write them down and walk to the first
actions.why: If you have to get out in a hurry or cannot get home, an agreed place tells everyone where to go and shows in seconds whether everyone is out.
actions.how: Pick a fixed place just outside your building that everyone can find in the dark: a named street corner, a particular store door or a bus shelter across the street. Stand there and look up, and move it if you are under windows, balconies or signs, or beside the main entrance, the garage ramp or a fire hydrant. Pick somewhere a wheelchair or stroller can reach, with cover from rain if you can. Pick a second place 1 to 3 miles away, outside your neighborhood, that everyone can reach on foot or by a route they already use and that is open long hours, such as a library, a community center or a relative's home. Agree how long to wait at each place and when to come back and check, for example on the hour. Write both places, the second one's address and your out-of-area contact's name and number (U2-155) on the Meeting places sheet. Put one copy on the fridge and one in each grab bag. Walk from the bedrooms to the first place together, once in daylight and once after dark with a flashlight; the two ways out of each room are in X2-09. If you ever leave separately, go to the meeting place and wait; do not go back inside to look for someone, tell the firefighters instead.
actions.done: The Meeting places sheet on the fridge and in each grab bag shows both places, your out-of-area contact and how long to wait, and everyone has walked to the first place in daylight and after dark.
actions.apartment: Beside a tall building, put the first place across the street or at the corner, not at the entrance, which fire crews need and where glass can fall; your ways down are the stairwells, never the elevator.
actions.cite_todo: An official source for standing clear of a tall building's facade because of falling glass, and for keeping the entrance clear for emergency vehicles.

actions.title: Move your meeting point clear of glass and the front entrance
actions.why: The pavement at the foot of a tall building is where broken glass lands and where fire engines pull up.
actions.how: Stand at your meeting place and look up. If you are under windows, balconies or signs, or beside the main entrance, the garage ramp or a fire hydrant, choose a new spot across the street or at the nearest corner. Pick somewhere a wheelchair or stroller can reach, with cover from rain if you can. Change it by hand on your Meeting places sheet; the site only records that it is done.
actions.done: You have stood at the meeting place and looked up, and the spot on your Meeting places sheet is clear of windows, balconies, signs and the main entrance.
actions.cite_todo: An official source for standing clear of a tall building's facade because of falling glass, and for keeping the entrance clear for emergency vehicles.

actions.title: Choose a second meeting place outside your neighborhood
actions.why: If your street is closed off, a place a short journey away gives everyone somewhere to head for without a phone call.
actions.how: Pick a place 1 to 3 miles (2 to 5 km) away that every household member can reach on foot or by a route they already use, and that is open long hours: a library, a relative's home, a place of worship. Agree how long to wait there and when to come back and check, for example on the hour. Write its name and address by hand on the Meeting places sheet; this site only records that it is done.
actions.done: The second meeting place's name and address are written on the Meeting places sheet, and everyone at home has heard how long to wait there.

actions.title: Write down when you stay and when you leave
actions.why: A rule agreed calmly in advance ends the argument at the door, because when a line you drew is crossed, you go.
actions.how: Agree the rule with everyone at home: you stay while the building is sound, the air is safe to breathe and you can keep the home at a safe temperature. You leave at once on an official evacuation order, a fire in your own home, a gas smell or structural damage, and if you feel unsafe you do not wait to be told. For a fire somewhere else in a tall building, follow HR-06, which in a fire-resistive building usually means staying in your home behind the closed door. If you live within 10 miles of a nuclear plant, an official order to stay indoors comes first in an emergency there, and you leave only when officials advise it (AR-12). On your local emergency office's website, find the words it uses for 'get ready' and 'go now', and whether your address is in a named evacuation zone. On the Our reasons to leave sheet, write your own line for each slower case: the room you live in stays above about 88 °F (31 °C) and someone at higher risk is with you (an older adult, a baby, a child under 5, someone pregnant or ill); you cannot keep warm with layers and blankets; there is smoke indoors; your stored water will run out before you can get more; a medical device cannot be kept powered. This site's suggestion for a seventh line: the elevators are out, you live high up and someone at home cannot walk the stairs on their own, such as a small child, so you go while it is light and the stairwell lights still work (PL-08). Beside each line, write where you would go (X2-03). On the Evacuation plan sheet, write your zone at the top and, under WHEN, one trigger for each hazard on your list, short enough to read in ten seconds, such as a warning for your zone or water in your street for a flood. People nearly always leave later than they meant to, so when a line is crossed, go without reopening the debate.
actions.done: The Our reasons to leave sheet lists your lines with a place to go beside each, and the Evacuation plan sheet shows your evacuation zone, or says your address has none, and a trigger for each hazard.

actions.title: Name the place you would go first
actions.why: A spare room with someone you know is easier than a public shelter, above all with children, pets or health needs.
actions.how: Think of one friend or relative outside your neighborhood whose home you could reach and stay in for a few nights. Write their name, address and phone by hand on the Evacuation plan sheet as your first choice. Public shelters are the fallback: they open only after an emergency starts, so note how your city announces them. The site only records that the sheet is done.
actions.done: A friend's or relative's name, address and phone are written on the Evacuation plan sheet as your first choice, with a note of how your city announces shelters.

actions.title: Choose two places to go if your building is unusable, and ask them now
actions.why: A building can be closed by fire, flood or a long outage while your own home is undamaged, and a host who has already said yes saves hours of phone calls.
actions.how: Pick two households: one you can walk to in under an hour, and one far enough away that the same outage or flood is unlikely to reach it. Ask each one now whether you could stay a few nights, and whether two weeks would be possible if it came to that, and offer the same in return. Check they can take your pets and that you can manage their stairs. Write both by hand on the Evacuation plan sheet. Agree how you would tell them you are coming if phones are down. The sheet has a third row: use it for a place in a different direction, or for the public shelter option for your area (U6-16).
actions.done: Two households have said yes to having you stay, and both are written on the Evacuation plan sheet.

actions.title: Write three ways to travel and what each needs ready
actions.why: The way you normally travel may be the first thing to stop working, and choosing a replacement under pressure costs time you may not have.
actions.how: On the Evacuation plan sheet, under HOW, write a first choice and two backups for reaching your first-choice place, each a different kind of transport: for example car, then a named bus or train line, then on foot or by bike. For each, ask what would stop it, such as a closed line, gridlock or a garage gate with no power. Beside each, write what must be ready: at least half a tank of gas, a transit card with credit, walking shoes and a paper map. Note who could give you a ride and whom you could take.
actions.done: A first choice and two backups, each a different kind of transport, are written under HOW on the Evacuation plan sheet with what must be ready for each.
actions.apartment: Many city households have no car, so make walking and transit your first two choices and a ride from a named person the third (X2-04); if you have a car in a garage, find out how it gets out when the electric gate has no power.

actions.title: Plan how you would leave without a car
actions.why: Buses and trains may stop in the very emergencies that make people leave, and a ride arranged in advance is far easier to get than one requested on the day.
actions.how: On the Evacuation plan sheet, write by hand three options: the walking route to your first-choice place with its distance, the transit lines that go there, and a named neighbor, friend or relative with a car who has agreed to take you. Ask that person this week. If anyone at home could not walk the route or manage the stairs, call your city's non-emergency line (311 in many US cities) or its emergency management office, ask whether it keeps a register of people who need transport in an evacuation, and sign up.
actions.done: The Evacuation plan sheet shows the walking route with its distance, the transit lines, and a named person with a car who has said yes to taking you.

actions.title: Decide who you tell when you leave
actions.why: People who know you have left stop searching for you, and rescuers do not spend time on an empty home.
actions.how: On the Evacuation plan sheet, write by hand the three people you will text when you leave: your out-of-area contact, the household you are heading to, and one neighbor or the building manager. Agree the message now: who is with you, where you are going and how, for example 'All 3 of us and the cat OK, walking to Sam's'. Do not count a text as received until you get a reply.
actions.done: The three people you will text are written on the Evacuation plan sheet, and everyone at home has heard the message you will send.

actions.title: Write a get-home plan for each commuter
actions.why: Emergencies often start while the household is spread across the city, and transit can stop with no warning.
actions.how: For each person who travels to work or school, print the Get-home plan and fill it in by hand: the walking route home, its distance and how long it would take, and two or three places to rest on the way, such as a friend's home or a library. Plan on 2 miles an hour for an adult with a bag and stops; that speed is this site's assumption, not an official figure. With children, time your own family over one mile and use that. Write the first rule at the top: if the building you are in is safe, stay there, tell your household you are safe, and set off in daylight once the streets are calmer. Add a second route that avoids any bridge or tunnel that could be closed. Find one colleague who lives your way and agree to walk together. Keep one copy at work, with the small kit there (X2-07), and one at home.
actions.done: Each commuter has a filled-in Get-home plan at work, and a second copy is at home.

actions.title: Agree who collects the children, and a family password
actions.why: Schools release children only to adults they know are authorized, and in an emergency that adult may not be you.
actions.how: Ask each school, childcare and after-school program for its emergency and reunification plan: where children are taken and what ID a collecting adult must show. Give them the names of two adults besides you who may collect your child, and tell your child who they are. Use a family password as one extra check, never as the only one; the school's own release rules decide who may collect a child, and a child who is unsure stays with staff. Write the reunification site and phone number by hand on each child's Emergency numbers sheet; the site only records that it is done.
actions.done: Each school and childcare has two more adults' names on file, your child can name them and say the family password, and the reunification site is on the child's Emergency numbers sheet.

actions.title: Keep a small kit at work
actions.why: If you have to stay put overnight or walk home, what is in your desk or locker is all you will have.
actions.how: In a drawer, locker or small bag at work, keep walking shoes and socks, about a quart of water, three snack bars, a phone cable and a charged power bank, one day of any medicine you take, and a small flashlight. Add a warm layer in winter and a sun hat in summer. Replace the water, snacks and medicine every 6 months.
actions.done: The shoes, water, snacks, medicine, cable, charged power bank and flashlight are in your drawer or locker at work, and the flashlight and power bank both work.

actions.title: Write down what would make you leave a building with no power
actions.why: Staying home is usually right in an outage, but some conditions make it dangerous, and tired people notice them late.
actions.how: Print the Our reasons to leave sheet and write your list by hand. Start with these six: the room you live in stays above about 31 °C (88 °F) and someone at higher risk is with you (an older adult, a baby, a child under 5, someone pregnant or ill); you cannot keep warm with layers and blankets; there is smoke indoors; your stored water will run out before you can get more; the building has new cracks or other damage; a medical device cannot be kept powered. Beside each, write where you would go. Agree that when any one is met you leave without reopening the debate; the site only records that the list is made.
actions.done: The Our reasons to leave sheet lists your reasons with a place to go beside each, and everyone at home has agreed to leave when one is met.

actions.title: Keep the plan on paper and offline on every phone
actions.why: A plan stored only online is out of reach exactly when networks and batteries fail.
actions.how: Put the filled-in Meeting places sheet, Evacuation plan sheet and Get-home plan in a folder by the door, with a copy in each grab bag. On each phone, photograph those three sheets and save the photos somewhere that opens with no signal; test it in airplane mode. Do not photograph the Bank and bills list or the medical sheets. Redo the photos whenever a sheet changes.
actions.done: The three sheets are in a folder by the door and in each grab bag, and their photos open on every phone in airplane mode.

actions.title: Add relatives and close friends to each Emergency numbers sheet
actions.why: Few people can recite more than one or two phone numbers from memory.
actions.how: On each person's Emergency numbers sheet, fill in the relative and friend rows: name, mobile number and who they are. Include at least one person nearby who holds a spare key or could reach your home on foot. Copy the numbers by hand from your phone and keep the sheets yourself; the site only records that it is done.
actions.done: The relative and friend rows on each person's Emergency numbers sheet are filled in, including one person nearby who holds a spare key or could walk to your home.

actions.title: Add your out-of-area contact to every sheet and phone
actions.why: The contact only works if every person can find the number without asking someone else.
actions.how: Write your out-of-area contact's name, mobile, landline and email by hand at the top of every Emergency numbers sheet. Save the same person in each phone with 'ICE' (in case of emergency) in front of the name. Agree the routine: after any emergency each person texts the contact 'I'm OK' and where they are, and the contact passes the messages on. The site only records that it is done.
actions.done: Your out-of-area contact is written at the top of every Emergency numbers sheet and saved in each phone with ICE in front of the name.

actions.title: Find your shut-offs: breaker panel, water valves, and gas valve if you have one
actions.why: A burst hose or a sparking socket stays a small problem if you can cut it off in seconds.
actions.how: Find the breaker panel: a metal door in a hallway, closet or kitchen, with the main switch at the top. Find the small stop valves under each sink and behind the toilet, and turn one clockwise and back to check that it moves. If you have a gas stove or dryer, find the lever valve on the pipe behind it; it is off when the lever sits crosswise to the pipe. In a house, also find the main water valve and the valve at the gas meter. Leaving comes before any valve: if you smell gas or hear hissing, follow the gas steps (AR-13).
actions.done: You have touched the breaker panel, turned one water stop valve and back, and found the gas valve or confirmed there is none.
actions.apartment: You control only your own panel, fixture valves and appliance gas valve; the building's main water, gas and electrical shut-offs are the building's, so leave them alone and know management's after-hours number.

actions.title: Sketch your home and mark the first-aid kit
actions.why: A kit that a guest, a babysitter or a child cannot find in the dark is of little use.
actions.how: Draw a rough floor plan of your home on one sheet of paper: rooms, doors and windows. Mark where the first-aid kit is kept with a cross and the letters FA. Keep the kit where an adult can reach it without a stool, such as a hall closet shelf, and tape the sketch inside that closet door.
actions.done: The sketch is taped inside the closet door with the first-aid kit marked FA, and the kit sits where an adult can reach it without a stool.

actions.title: Keep the bags by the way out and mark them on the sketch
actions.why: A bag at the back of a closet gets left behind when you have two minutes to go.
actions.how: Keep every person's bag in the same place, within a few steps of the door you would leave by: a hall closet floor or hooks by the door. Mark the spot on your home sketch with the word BAGS. Tell everyone at home, and check that nothing is stacked in front of them.
actions.done: Every bag sits within a few steps of the door you would leave by, with nothing stacked in front, and the spot is marked BAGS on your sketch.

actions.title: Mark every smoke alarm on the sketch and note the gaps
actions.why: A smoke alarm gives you the minutes you need to get out, but only if there is a working one near where people sleep.
actions.how: Walk through your home and mark each smoke alarm on your sketch. You should find one inside each bedroom, one outside each sleeping area and one on every level. Press each test button, and read the date on the back: an alarm more than 10 years old needs replacing. In a rented home, report a missing or dead alarm to the landlord in writing today.
actions.done: Every smoke alarm is marked on your sketch and sounded when tested, and any missing, dead or out-of-date alarm is noted and, in a rented home, reported to the landlord in writing.
actions.apartment: Alarms in corridors and stairwells belong to the building; if one is chirping or missing, tell management.

actions.title: Mark the fire extinguishers on the sketch and check them
actions.why: You have only seconds to reach an extinguisher while a fire is still small enough to put out.
actions.how: Mark any extinguisher in your home on the sketch; the best place for one is near the kitchen door on your way out, not beside the stove. Check that the gauge needle is in the green and the pin is in place. Use it only on a small fire that is not spreading, once everyone else is leaving and the fire department has been called, with your back to a clear exit: pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze, sweep. If the fire does not go out at once, leave and close the door behind you.
actions.done: Your sketch shows where each extinguisher is, or that you have none, and each one you own has its gauge needle in the green and its pin in place.
actions.apartment: Also mark the nearest extinguisher cabinet, hose reel and alarm pull station in your corridor; they belong to the building and are there for residents to use.

actions.title: Plan for the mobility aids you rely on
actions.why: A wheelchair, walker or scooter that is damaged, out of charge or left upstairs changes what you can do for yourself.
actions.how: Label each aid with your name and a phone number. Keep its charger, a spare battery if it takes one, and a tire repair kit or spare tips together in one bag. Keep a simple backup for when the main aid fails or cannot come with you: a folding manual chair, a walker or a cane. If you cannot manage stairs, tell building management, agree with two neighbors who will come to you, and decide where you will wait for firefighters.
actions.done: Each aid is labeled, its charger and spares are in one bag, a backup aid is at home, and if you cannot manage stairs two neighbors have agreed to come to you.
actions.apartment: With no elevator, a powered chair stays on your floor, so plan what you would use once you reach street level.

actions.title: Plan for hearing, vision and communication aids
actions.why: Warnings, instructions and offers of help all arrive as sound or text, and an aid with a dead battery cuts you off from them.
actions.how: List the aids each person uses: hearing aids, a cochlear processor, glasses, a white cane, a screen reader, a communication board or device. For each one, keep at least one unopened pack of spare batteries, or a charger and cable, in your bag. Set up alerts in a form that works for you: flashing and vibrating phone alerts, a weather radio with a strobe or bed shaker, or text alerts read aloud. Carry a printed card that says how you communicate best, in case the device is lost.
actions.done: Spare batteries or a charger for each aid and a printed card saying how you communicate best are in your bag, and your phone or radio alerts flash, vibrate or speak.

actions.title: Arrange backup power for any device someone depends on
actions.why: A breathing machine, powered chair, feeding pump or medicine fridge stops when the power does, and an outage can last for days.
actions.how: For each device, read the watts on its label and ask the supplier how long its own battery lasts and which backup battery the maker approves; the site adds up the watt-hours from your power audit. Tell your electricity company that someone at home depends on powered medical equipment and ask to join its medical or priority register. Get a backup battery or power station that covers at least one night, and test it. Decide now where you will go when it runs low, and never run a fuel generator indoors, on a balcony or closer than 20 feet (6 m) to the building.
actions.done: Every powered medical device has a tested backup that lasts at least one night and the electricity company knows about it.
actions.apartment: A fuel generator cannot be used in an apartment or on a balcony, so a battery is the only backup power you can run indoors.

actions.title: Put a spare pair of glasses in your bag
actions.why: If your only pair breaks or is left behind, reading a label, a map or a phone screen becomes hard.
actions.how: Put your previous pair of glasses in a hard case in your bag, even if the prescription is a little old. If you wear contact lenses, add a spare pair, a travel bottle of solution and a case, and still pack glasses. Keep a copy of your current prescription with your documents so that a replacement can be ordered anywhere.
actions.done: Your spare glasses are in a hard case in your bag, and a copy of your current prescription is with your documents.

actions.title: List each medical device and plan its backup power
actions.why: A device someone needs to breathe, move or get treatment stops when the power does, and a supplier can replace or reset it quickly only if they know exactly which one it is.
actions.how: On the One-page medical summary, write each device the household relies on, such as hearing aids, a powered wheelchair or scooter, a stair lift, CPAP, an oxygen concentrator, a nebulizer, a powered bed, a glucose monitor, or a feeding or infusion pump. For each, write the maker, model and serial number, its prescribed settings, the supplier's phone and out-of-hours line, and your account number. Add two or three lines on how to operate it, plain enough for a stranger to follow, and photograph the label on the device. Beside each, write whether it runs on wall power, batteries (and which size) or neither, and mark any that someone could not go 24 hours without. For each powered device, read the watts on its label and ask the supplier how long its own battery lasts, which backup battery the maker approves, and what they do for customers in a long outage. Get a backup battery or power station that covers at least one night, test it, and write the battery hours beside the device. Ask each clinic, supplier or home-care agency you rely on what happens if it loses power or you cannot reach it, which other site would treat you, who contacts whom, and how many days of supplies to keep at home. Tell your electricity company that someone at home depends on powered medical equipment and ask to join its medical or priority list; this does not guarantee power, so you still need the backup. Decide now where you would go while battery hours are left: a relative with power, a shelter with power, or a hospital. Never run a fuel generator indoors, on a balcony or closer than 20 feet to the building. If a life-sustaining device loses power and you have no backup, call 911 right away. Keep the summary with the device, with one copy by the door and one in your bag.
actions.done: The medical summary kept with the device lists each device's maker, model, serial number, supplier, power source and battery hours, every powered device has a tested backup that lasts at least one night, and the electricity company has been told.
actions.apartment: In an apartment a battery is the only backup power you can run, and with the elevators out you may not be able to leave quickly, so tell building management which unit has someone on powered medical equipment and plan to leave early, while you still have battery hours.

actions.title: Write a one-page note that tells helpers how to help you
actions.why: A firefighter, shelter worker or neighbor can help you properly only if they know what you need, and you may not be able to tell them.
actions.how: Print the Care instructions sheet and write by hand: the languages you speak and how you communicate best, the conditions and allergies a helper must know about, the help you need with moving, eating or medicines, and two people to notify. Keep it to one page in plain words. Put one copy in your bag and one by the door; the site only records that you wrote it.
actions.done: Anyone who needs help from responders has a one-page note saying how to help them.

actions.title: Set aside diapers, continence and other personal hygiene supplies
actions.why: These are among the first things to run out, and stores may be closed or empty for days.
actions.how: Count what each person uses on a normal day: diapers or pull-ups, continence pads, catheter or ostomy supplies, period products, wipes. Multiply by 3 and set that much aside now, then build up to your target days by buying one extra pack on each shopping trip. Stay with the brand and size you already use, and add bags that tie shut for disposal.
actions.done: Three times each person's daily count is set aside, in the brand and size they already use, with bags that tie shut for disposal.

actions.title: Ask three people to be your support network
actions.why: Neighbors and friends reach people long before emergency services can, and they can help in the way you need only if you have shown them.
actions.how: Choose at least three people who are usually nearby at different times of day: a neighbor on your floor, a friend or relative, a co-worker. Ask each one directly whether they will check on you in an emergency, and show them where your medicines and equipment are, how to move you or your chair, and how any device works. Give one of them a spare key, swap phone numbers on paper, and agree that they come without waiting for a call if phones are down. Offer the same in return.
actions.done: Three people have said yes, each has been shown your medicines and equipment, one holds a spare key, and you hold each other's numbers on paper.

actions.title: Post a One-page medical summary where responders will see it
actions.why: Responders who find someone unable to speak can act faster with that person's medicines, equipment and contacts in front of them.
actions.how: Fill in a One-page medical summary by hand for each person who needs one: medicines and doses, allergies, conditions, equipment used, doctor and two emergency contacts. Put it in a clear plastic sleeve and fix it to the fridge door or the inside of your front door at eye level. Write the date on it and replace it whenever a medicine changes.
actions.done: A dated medical information sheet is posted inside the front door or on the fridge for each person who needs one.

actions.title: Sign up for alerts in a form you can use
actions.why: An alert you cannot hear, see or read gives no warning at all.
actions.how: On your city or county emergency management website, register every way it offers that works for you: text, voice call, email, landline or TTY. Register someone from your support network at your address as well, so they get the same warnings. On your phone, open Accessibility in Settings and turn on flashing or vibrating alerts and spoken notifications. Ask the office whether it keeps a register of residents who need extra help in an evacuation, and join it.
actions.done: Your local alert system has confirmed your registration and your support person's, and your phone flashes, vibrates or speaks when an alert arrives.

actions.title: Find a second and third place for treatment you cannot miss
actions.why: If your usual clinic is closed or out of reach, missing dialysis, infusions or oxygen deliveries can become dangerous within days.
actions.how: Ask your clinic or supplier what its emergency plan is and where you should go if it is closed. Write by hand on your One-page medical summary the names, addresses and phone numbers of two other sites that can treat you, one of them in a different part of the city. Ask whether they need a referral or your records in advance, and what to do if you miss a session.
actions.done: Two other places that can give any treatment you cannot miss are written on the medical summary.

actions.title: Wear a medical alert tag or bracelet
actions.why: A tag speaks for you when you cannot speak for yourself.
actions.how: If you have a condition, allergy, implant or medicine that would change emergency treatment, order an engraved bracelet or necklace. Have it engraved with the condition, the critical allergy or medicine, and an emergency contact number. Wear it every day, and fill in the emergency medical ID on your phone so that both say the same thing.
actions.done: The engraved tag is on your wrist or neck, and the medical ID on your phone says the same thing.

actions.title: Tag, chip and crate each pet, and fill in its Pet sheet
actions.why: A frightened animal that slips away gets home fastest when a stranger can read a number or scan a chip, and shelters, hotels and helpers usually take an animal only if it is contained and its records come with it.
actions.how: Fit an engraved tag with your pet's name, your cell number and your out-of-area contact's to a collar or harness it wears all the time, snug enough that only two fingers fit underneath; indoor cats need one too, on a breakaway collar. Ask your vet or a local animal shelter to microchip the pet, and register the chip with your cell, your email and a second contact outside your area; if it is already chipped, check the registry's details today. Get one carrier per animal, big enough for it to stand up and turn around in, and write your name, your cell number, the pet's name and the vet's number on it in permanent marker. Leave the carrier out for a week with the door open and a blanket inside, then store it beside your bags. For a dog too big to carry, keep a strong leash, and a muzzle if it may bite when frightened. Keep a spare leash and a fitted harness or collar with the pet bag; for a cat, a harness as well as the carrier. On a Pet sheet for each animal, write its name, species, breed, age, sex and color, the chip number, your vet and the nearest 24-hour emergency vet, its vaccination dates, its feeding routine, each condition and medicine with the dose and time your vet set, any allergies, and how it behaves under stress. If you wish, add a signed line giving permission for treatment up to an amount you choose. Clip on the vet's printed vaccination record and two dated photos: a side view that shows its markings and one with you beside the animal. Tape a copy of the sheet in a plastic bag to the carrier. What goes in the pet bag itself is in BG-11. Check the tag and the harness fit every 6 months, and retake the photos once a year.
actions.done: Each pet wears a readable tag with two numbers, the chip registry shows your current details, and its labeled carrier is stored beside your bags with a filled-in Pet sheet taped to it.
actions.apartment: Check that you can carry the loaded carrier down your stairs with one hand free for the rail; a backpack-style carrier makes this easier.

actions.title: Microchip your pet and check the registration
actions.why: Collars come off, and a chip stays with the animal, but it only works if the registry holds your current number.
actions.how: Ask your vet or a local animal shelter to implant a microchip; it takes a few minutes at a normal visit. Register the chip number with your mobile, your email and a second contact outside your area. If your pet is already chipped, log in to the registry today to check the details, and ask the vet to scan the chip at the next visit. Write the chip number by hand on the Pet sheet; the site only records that it is done.
actions.done: The chip registry shows your current mobile, email and a second contact outside your area, and the chip number is written on the Pet sheet.

actions.title: Write down each pet's age, vet and vaccinations
actions.why: Shelters, kennels and hotels often ask for proof of vaccination before they will take an animal.
actions.how: Print a Pet sheet for each animal and write by hand its name, species, breed, age, sex and color, the vet's name and phone, and the dates of its last vaccinations. Ask the vet for a printed vaccination record and clip it to the sheet. Keep it yourself; this site only records that it is done.
actions.done: Each animal has a Pet sheet with its details, vet and vaccination dates written in and the vet's printed vaccination record clipped on.

actions.title: Take a current photo of each pet, and one with you in it
actions.why: A recent photo is how you describe a lost animal, and a photo of the two of you together helps show that it is yours.
actions.how: Take two photos of each pet today: a clear side view that shows its markings, and one with you beside the animal. Print both, write the date on the back and clip them to the Pet sheet; keep copies on your phone. Retake them once a year. This site stores no photos and only records that it is done.
actions.done: Two dated prints for each pet, a side view and one with you beside it, are clipped to the Pet sheet, with copies on your phone.

actions.title: Get a carrier or crate for each pet and label it
actions.why: Shelters, hotels and friends offering a lift will usually take an animal only if it is contained.
actions.how: Get one carrier per animal, big enough for it to stand up and turn around in. Write your name, your mobile number and the pet's name on it in permanent marker. Leave it out for a week with the door open and a blanket inside so that it becomes a familiar place, then store it beside your bags. For a dog too big to carry, pack a strong leash, and a muzzle if it may bite when frightened.
actions.done: Each pet's labeled carrier, big enough for it to stand and turn around, is stored beside your bags, or a strong leash is packed for a dog too big to carry.
actions.apartment: Check that you can carry the loaded carrier down your stairs with one hand free for the rail; a backpack-style carrier makes this easier.

actions.title: Pack three days of pet food in the pet bag
actions.why: A sudden change of food upsets an animal's stomach at the worst possible time, and a shelter may have none to give.
actions.how: Measure what your pet eats in a day and pack 3 days of the same food: dry food in a sealed bag or screw-top tub, or pull-tab cans with a spoon. Write the daily amount on the bag. Add at least 3 days of any medicine the animal takes, more if your vet will supply it. Swap the food for fresh every 6 months.
actions.done: Three days of your pet's usual food is in the pet bag with the daily amount written on it, along with at least 3 days of any medicine it takes.

actions.title: Keep a spare leash, collar and harness with the pet bag
actions.why: The leash you use every day will not be by the door at 3 a.m., and a panicking animal can back out of a loose collar.
actions.how: Put a spare leash and a correctly fitted harness or collar in the pet bag; a harness is harder to slip than a collar. For a cat, pack a harness as well as the carrier. Check the fit twice a year, because animals change size.
actions.done: A spare leash and a harness or collar that fits your pet today are in the pet bag.

actions.title: Pack water for your pet
actions.why: An animal on a long walk or in a crowded shelter needs water as much as you do, and may not be offered any.
actions.how: Put at least 1 liter (about a quart) of sealed water per pet in the pet bag, and 2 liters for a large dog. That is for the journey, and you refill it when you can; your home store covers the rest. The site's calculator plans half a gallon (about 2 liters) per pet per day for the home store; that figure is this site's assumption, not an official one, so ask your vet what your own animal needs. Replace sealed bottles by the date printed on them.
actions.done: At least 1 liter of sealed water per pet, or 2 liters for a large dog, is in the pet bag.
actions.cite_todo: An official figure for how much drinking water a pet needs per day by size. Ready.gov's pets page gives no daily amount, so the half gallon per pet per day used for home storage is this site's assumption (D-09), and the amounts for the bag are a carrying compromise.

actions.title: Pack a food bowl and a water bowl
actions.why: Many animals will not drink from a bottle or a cupped hand, and nobody will lend you a dish.
actions.how: Put two light bowls in the pet bag, one for food and one for water; collapsible ones weigh almost nothing and clip to the outside. Let your pet use them at home a few times so that they are familiar.
actions.done: Two light bowls are in or clipped to the pet bag, and your pet has eaten and drunk from them at home.

actions.title: Pack absorbent pads for the carrier
actions.why: An animal shut in a carrier for hours will soil it, and a dry pad keeps it clean and calmer.
actions.how: Line the carrier with one absorbent training pad and pack 6 more, about two a day for 3 days. Add a small pack of unscented wipes. For a dog that normally goes outdoors, the pads also give it somewhere to go if you are kept inside.
actions.done: One absorbent pad lines the carrier, and 6 more and a small pack of unscented wipes are packed with it.

actions.title: Pack litter and a small tray
actions.why: A cat with nowhere to go will hold on until it is ill, or use your host's floor.
actions.how: Pack a folding or disposable litter tray and about 2 kg (4 to 5 lb) of the litter your cat already uses in a sealed bag, enough for a thin layer for about 3 days. Add a scoop and a few small bags for waste. If you have no tray, a shallow cardboard box lined with a trash bag will do.
actions.done: A small tray, about 2 kg of your cat's usual litter in a sealed bag, a scoop and waste bags are packed with the pet bag.

actions.title: Add a familiar toy and bedding
actions.why: Something that smells of home settles an animal in a strange place better than anything you can buy.
actions.how: Put one favorite toy or chew and a small blanket or towel your pet has slept on into the carrier or pet bag. Do not wash the blanket first, since the smell is the point. For a caged bird or small animal, add a cloth to cover the cage.
actions.done: One favorite toy or chew and an unwashed blanket or towel your pet has slept on are in the carrier or pet bag.

actions.title: Pack bags for cleaning up after your pet
actions.why: You will be expected to clean up after your animal wherever you stay.
actions.how: Pack a roll of at least 20 waste bags, 5 larger trash bags for used litter or pads, and 5 pairs of disposable gloves. Tie each bag shut, put it inside a second bag, and use an outdoor bin. Never flush litter or bags.
actions.done: A roll of at least 20 waste bags, 5 larger trash bags and 5 pairs of disposable gloves are in the pet bag.

actions.title: Write down your pet's feeding routine
actions.why: Someone else may have to feed your pet if you are in hospital, kept out of the area, or in a shelter that houses animals separately.
actions.how: On the Pet sheet, write by hand what your pet eats (brand and type), how much, how many times a day and at what times, and any food it must never have. Put a copy in a plastic bag taped to the carrier. This site only records that it is done.
actions.done: The feeding routine is written on the Pet sheet, and a copy in a plastic bag is taped to the carrier.

actions.title: Write down your pet's medical conditions and medicines
actions.why: A carer who does not know about a condition or a daily tablet cannot keep your animal well.
actions.how: On the Pet sheet, write by hand each condition, each medicine with its dose and time of day, and any allergies. Note where the medicine is kept and how you get the animal to take it. Keep a copy with the carrier; the site only records that you did it.
actions.done: The Pet sheet lists each condition, each medicine with its dose and time, and any allergies, or says there are none, and a copy is with the carrier.

actions.title: Write down how your pet behaves under stress
actions.why: A handler who knows that an animal bites when cornered or bolts through open doors can keep it, and themselves, safe.
actions.how: On the Pet sheet, write by hand anything a stranger should know: fear of men, children, other animals or loud noise; biting, scratching or escaping; what calms it and the words it responds to. Be frank, because the note protects your pet. Keep a copy with the carrier; this site only records that it is done.
actions.done: What a stranger should know about your pet under stress is written on the Pet sheet, and a copy is with the carrier.

actions.title: Write your vet's name and number on the sheet and the carrier
actions.why: Whoever is holding your pet may need its records or urgent advice when you cannot be reached.
actions.how: On the Pet sheet, write by hand your vet's name, clinic, address and phone, and the nearest 24-hour emergency vet. If you wish, add a signed line giving permission for treatment up to an amount you choose. Write the vet's number on the carrier label as well; the site only records that it is done.
actions.done: Your vet and the nearest 24-hour emergency vet are written on the Pet sheet, and the vet's number is on the carrier label.

actions.title: List two boarding kennels that could take your pet
actions.why: If you have to go somewhere animals cannot, a kennel you have already checked is far better than leaving a pet behind.
actions.how: Find two kennels, catteries or vets that board animals: one near home and one 30 miles or more away in the direction you would travel. Phone each and ask which vaccinations and papers it requires, what a night costs, and whether it stays open in emergencies. Write the names, addresses and phone numbers by hand on the back of the Pet sheet.
actions.done: Two boarding places you have phoned, one near home and one 30 miles or more away, are written on the back of the Pet sheet.

actions.title: List pet-friendly hotels on your way out of the area
actions.why: Ready.gov and CDC say many public shelters do not take pets, while the Red Cross says its shelters welcome pets, which may be housed nearby, so a hotel that has already agreed to take your animal is worth having on your list.
actions.how: Find at least three hotels or motels that accept pets, near each place you would evacuate to and along the routes there. Phone to confirm the rule for your animal's size and species, the fee, and whether a no-pets rule is waived in a declared emergency. Write the names, addresses and phone numbers by hand on the back of the Pet sheet.
actions.done: At least three hotels that confirmed by phone they take your pet are written on the back of the Pet sheet.

actions.title: Find out which hazards apply to your address
actions.why: You can only plan for what is likely where you live, and the list for a riverside flat differs from the list for one on a hill.
actions.how: Open your city or county emergency management website and find its hazard list or hazard map. Enter your address in any flood, wildfire, tsunami or evacuation-zone map it links to. Write down the three most likely emergencies for your address and season, for example a long power cut, extreme heat, flooding or wildfire smoke, and keep the list with your plan. If you cannot find it online, phone the office or the fire department's non-emergency line and ask.
actions.done: A written list of the three most likely emergencies for your address is kept with your plan.

actions.title: Walk through your home looking for things that could hurt you
actions.why: Many injuries at home in an emergency come from ordinary things such as falling furniture, broken glass and blocked exits.
actions.how: Go room by room with a notepad. Look for heavy things above beds and sofas, tall furniture not fixed to the wall, anything in the way between each bed and the front door, overloaded extension leads, and anything that can burn within 3 feet (1 m) of a heater. Check that each window you might need opens. Fix what takes minutes today and add the rest to your three-column list (U6-02).
actions.done: You have walked every room with a notepad, the quick fixes are done, and the rest are written on your three-column list.
actions.apartment: Include the corridor and stairs outside your door, and report anything stored there to management.

actions.title: Learn the ways a warning will reach you
actions.why: No single channel reaches everyone, so you need at least two that work when you are asleep and when the power is off.
actions.how: Check each of the four channels: alerts pushed to every cell phone in an area, your local sign-up alert system, radio and TV broadcasts, and outdoor sirens or building public-address systems where they exist. Ask your local emergency office which of these it uses and what its siren signals mean. Make sure one will wake you at night, such as a phone left on and charging by the bed, and one works with the power off, such as a battery radio.
actions.done: One warning channel that will wake you is set up by the bed, one works with the power off, and your emergency office has told you which channels it uses.

actions.title: Bookmark and follow your local emergency management office
actions.why: In an emergency the local office publishes the instructions that actually apply to your street.
actions.how: Search for the name of your city or county plus 'emergency management'. Save the official website to your phone's home screen. Follow its accounts on the social media you already use and turn on notifications for them, then do the same for your fire department and your electricity company.
actions.done: The emergency office's website is on your phone's home screen, and notifications are on for its accounts, your fire department's and your electricity company's.

actions.title: Register for local alerts at ORalert.gov
actions.why: Sign-up alerts carry local detail, such as evacuation zones and boil-water notices, that nationwide phone alerts leave out.
actions.how: Go to oralert.gov and enter your address; it passes you to your county's sign-up page. Add your mobile, email and any landline, and choose text messages. Add a second address, such as work or a relative's home. Update it whenever you move or change number.
actions.done: You have received the confirmation text or email from your county alert system, and a second address is on your account.

region.label: Oregon
region.general: Outside Oregon, sign up with your own city, county or state alert system; search for the place name plus 'emergency alerts'.

actions.title: Write your local news radio and TV stations on the radio
actions.why: When the internet is down, broadcast radio is often the last source of official news still working.
actions.how: Find the AM or FM frequency of two local stations that carry news and emergency announcements; your local emergency office can tell you which stations broadcast official alerts for your area. Write the station names and frequencies on a label, stick it on your battery radio, and note the main local TV news channel. Tune the radio to the first station now so that it is ready.
actions.done: A label with two station names and frequencies is stuck on your battery radio, and the radio is tuned to the first one.

actions.title: Find and set your weather radio channel
actions.why: Weather radio broadcasts official warnings around the clock and can sound an alarm while you sleep.
actions.how: In the United States, NOAA Weather Radio uses seven frequencies between 162.400 and 162.550 MHz; look up the one for your county on the National Weather Service website. Set your weather radio to that channel. If your radio has SAME county coding, enter your county's code from the same website, so that it sounds only for your area. Write the frequency on the radio. Elsewhere, write down the station your national weather or civil protection service uses.
actions.done: Your weather radio is set to your county's channel, with any county code entered, and the frequency is written on the radio.

actions.title: Check the emergency alert switches on every phone
actions.why: These alerts need no sign-up and no app, but one switched-off setting silences them.
actions.how: On an iPhone, open Settings, then Notifications, and scroll to Government Alerts at the bottom; on Android, open Settings and search for 'emergency alerts'. Turn on every type offered: extreme and severe threats, public safety messages and test alerts. Do this on each phone in the household, including children's and older relatives' phones. When severe weather is forecast, leave the phone on overnight and not in airplane mode.
actions.done: Every phone in the household, children's and older relatives' included, shows every emergency alert type switched on.

actions.title: Choose two more sources you trust and save them
actions.why: Rumors spread fast when people are frightened, and deciding in advance whom you believe keeps you from acting on one.
actions.how: Pick two sources besides the emergency office: for example the national weather service forecast for your area, your electricity company's outage map, your transit operator, or a local public radio newsroom. Save their websites and follow their official accounts. Agree at home that you act on these and on official alerts, and check anything else against them before passing it on.
actions.done: Two more sources are saved and followed on your phone, and everyone at home has heard which sources you act on.

actions.title: Test the whole plan once
actions.why: A plan that has never been tried always has a gap, and a quiet weekend is the time to find it.
actions.how: Pick an hour when everyone is home and say, without warning, 'we have to leave'. Each person takes their bag, you all go down the stairs to the outside meeting place, and one person texts the out-of-area contact; time it. Then walk or ride to the second meeting place. Write down what was slow, missing or forgotten, fix it, and set a date to repeat the test in 6 months.
actions.done: Everyone has walked with their bag to both meeting places, the contact has been texted, what went wrong is written down and fixed, and the next test is in the calendar.

actions.title: Volunteer with a group that helps after disasters
actions.why: Trained volunteers from groups such as CERT and the Red Cross run shelters and check on neighbors after a disaster, and the training makes your own household safer too.
actions.how: Pick one: your local Community Emergency Response Team (CERT), the Red Cross, a food bank, or a volunteer group registered with your city's emergency office. Go to one information session or take the free introductory course. Sign up before an emergency, because volunteers who are already registered and trained can be put to work right away.
actions.done: You have been to one information session or taken the introductory course, and your name is on the group's list of volunteers.

actions.title: Fill in the Household sheet for every person
actions.why: If someone is hurt or you are separated, a helper needs each person's number, birth date, medicines and allergies, and you may not be there to give them.
actions.how: Print the Household sheet. Write one row for each person who lives with you: full name, cell number, date of birth, medicines taken, allergies, and anything else a helper should know, such as a medical condition, school or workplace. Keep one copy with your documents and one in your bag. Set a yearly reminder to update it.
actions.done: Every person's row on the Household sheet is complete, one copy is with your documents and one in your bag, and a yearly reminder is set.

actions.title: Complete a Pet sheet for every animal
actions.why: One page with the license, microchip and vet details is what a shelter, kennel or finder needs to get your pet back to you.
actions.how: On each Pet sheet, fill in by hand the name, age, species and breed, license number, microchip number, vet's name and phone, and any medical or behavior notes. Clip on the vaccination record and the photos. Keep one copy with your documents and one with the carrier.
actions.done: Every animal's Pet sheet is filled in with its vaccination record and photos clipped on, with one copy in your documents and one with the carrier.

actions.title: Write your two meeting places and your out-of-area contact on one sheet
actions.why: Agreed places are forgotten within weeks unless they are written where everyone can see them.
actions.how: Print the Meeting places sheet and write by hand: the place just outside your building, the second place outside your neighborhood with its address, and your out-of-area contact's name and number. Add how long you wait at each place and when you come back to check. Put one copy on the fridge and one in each grab bag; the site only records that it is done.
actions.done: The Meeting places sheet shows both places, your out-of-area contact and your waiting times, with one copy on the fridge and one in each grab bag.

actions.title: Make an Emergency numbers sheet for each person in the household
actions.why: Your contact list is only as available as your phone, and each person's day involves different places and people, so a child's school is no use on someone else's list.
actions.how: Print one Emergency numbers sheet per person and write their name at the top. Fill in the rows that apply to them, each with a name and a phone number: work, school, childcare, babysitter, after-school program, doctor, pharmacy, eye doctor, landlord or building manager, any home-care or equipment supplier, your insurer's claims line, the utilities, and a place of worship. Fill in the relative and friend rows, including at least one person nearby who holds a spare key or could reach your home on foot. Copy the numbers from your phone, bills and prescription labels. Give each person their own sheet for their bag and keep a full set with your documents at home. Have each person memorize two numbers: the out-of-area contact and one household member.
actions.done: Each person has their own filled-in Emergency numbers sheet in their bag, a full set is kept with your documents, and each person can say two numbers from memory.

actions.title: Fill in the Insurance and legal list
actions.why: Claims, benefits and legal help all start with a company name and a phone number, and after a loss the policy papers may be gone.
actions.how: Print the Insurance and legal list. For every policy you hold (renters or home, health, car, life, disability, dental, vision, prescription, and any flood or earthquake insurance), write the company and its claims phone number, adding only the last four digits of the policy number if you need them to tell policies apart. You will find them on the first page of the policy, on your insurance card or in the insurer's app. Add a lawyer or legal aid contact if you have one. Put a line through the types you do not hold, and circle any you want to look into, such as renters insurance. Store it with your documents.
actions.done: Every policy you hold is on the Insurance and legal list with its claims phone number, and the list is stored with your documents.

actions.title: Fill in the Utilities list and save the outage numbers
actions.why: You cannot report an outage or a leak quickly if the number is on a website you cannot load or in a phone that is dead.
actions.how: Print the Utilities list. From a recent bill or the provider's website, copy for electricity, gas, water, sewer, phone, and cable and internet: the provider, its outage or emergency number, and the last four digits of each account you pay. Ask your gas, electricity and water providers where your shut-off is, whether you may turn it yourself, what tool it needs, and who turns it back on and how long that takes. Mark which services are in the landlord's or the building's name, and write the building's after-hours number in those rows. Add your city's non-emergency number (311 in many US cities). Bookmark each utility's outage map and save the numbers in every phone. Store the list with your documents and one recent bill, which also serves as proof of address. If you smell gas, follow the gas steps (AR-13).
actions.done: Every row of the Utilities list holds a provider's outage number or is marked as the building's with its after-hours number, the list is stored with a recent bill, and the outage maps are bookmarked on your phone.
actions.apartment: In many apartments the water, sewer and sometimes heat are in the building's name, so put the outage and shut-off questions to management: you can shut off only what is inside your unit (HR-15), and management or the utility shuts off everything else (HR-25).

actions.title: Lock the Bank and bills list away and tell one person where it is
actions.why: A list of your accounts helps you recover and would help a thief steal, so where it is kept matters as much as what is on it.
actions.how: Check that the Bank and bills list is complete: every bank, card, loan and pension, with its website and customer service number, and no passwords or PINs. Seal it in an envelope and keep it in a locked box or your document pouch, never on the fridge or as a photo on your phone. Tell one trusted person where it is. The list is handwritten and stays with you; this site only records that it is done.
actions.done: The complete Bank and bills list is sealed in an envelope in a locked box or your document pouch, and one trusted person has been told where it is.

actions.title: Write your reason to leave for each hazard
actions.why: A written rule ends the argument at the door, because when the condition is met you go.
actions.how: On the Evacuation plan sheet, under WHEN, write by hand one clear trigger for each hazard on your list. Examples: for fire, what your building's fire safety plan tells you to do when the alarm sounds; for flood, a warning for your zone or water in your street; for earthquake, new cracks, a gas smell or being told the building is unsafe; for any hazard, an official order to leave. Keep each one short enough to read in ten seconds. The site only records that it is done.
actions.done: One short trigger for each hazard on your list is written under WHEN on the Evacuation plan sheet.

actions.title: Write three ways to travel: a first choice and two backups
actions.why: Any one way of traveling can fail, and choosing a replacement under pressure costs time you may not have.
actions.how: On the Evacuation plan sheet, under HOW, write by hand a first choice and two backups, each a different kind of transport: for example car, then a named bus or train line, then on foot or by bike. Beside each, write what must be ready: at least half a tank of fuel, a transit card with credit, walking shoes and a paper map. Note who could give you a lift and whom you could take. The site only records that it is done.
actions.done: A first choice and two backups, each a different kind of transport, are written under HOW on the Evacuation plan sheet with what must be ready for each.
actions.apartment: With no car, make walking and transit your first two choices and a lift from a named person the third; if you have a car in a garage, find out how it gets out when the gate has no power.

actions.title: Write three places to go: a first choice and two backups
actions.why: Your first choice may be caught in the same emergency, so the plan needs somewhere further away.
actions.how: On the Evacuation plan sheet, under WHERE, write by hand three places with address and phone: a home within walking distance, a home in another part of the city or region, and a third in a different direction, or the public shelter option for your area. Phone each host to confirm, and note whether pets are welcome. The site only records that it is done.
actions.done: Three places with address and phone are written under WHERE on the Evacuation plan sheet, and each host has confirmed by phone.

actions.title: Catalog the belongings you would miss
actions.why: An insurer pays for what you can show you owned, and few people can list their possessions from memory after a loss.
actions.how: Print the Belongings catalog and start with the 10 most valuable or hardest-to-replace things you own. For each, write by hand what it is, the make and model, the serial number, where and when you bought it and what you paid, and tick the boxes once you have a photo and the receipt. Then film each room slowly, opening cupboards and drawers. Keep a copy of the sheet and the video away from home, for example with your out-of-area contact; this site stores neither and only records that it is done.
actions.done: The Belongings catalog lists your 10 most valuable or hardest-to-replace things, each room is on video, and a copy of both is kept away from home.
actions.apartment: If you rent, the landlord's insurance covers the building and not your things, so this list is what a renters or contents claim is built from.

actions.title: Brief your out-of-area contact, pick a backup and put them on every sheet
actions.why: The contact can pass messages between you only if they know the job and whom to expect, and every person can find their number without asking someone else.
actions.how: Start from the person you texted in U2-02, and check they live far enough away that the same storm, outage or earthquake is unlikely to reach them: another region or state, for example 100 miles or more. If you have a second home, check the contact is far from both; if nobody is, name one for each home and agree that, wherever you are, everyone texts the one who lives far from that home. Phone them and explain the job: after an emergency each of you texts or calls them to say you are safe and where you are, and they write it down and pass it on to the others. Ask them to save every household member's number under a clear name, and agree a second way to reach them, such as email or a messaging app. Choose a backup in a different place in case the first cannot be reached. Write both on the Wallet contact cards sheet, and the main contact's name, cell, landline and email at the top of every Emergency numbers sheet. Save the contact in each phone with 'ICE' (in case of emergency) in front of the name. Give the contact a paper list of the names and cell numbers from your Household sheet, your two meeting places and the address you would evacuate to, leaving off medical details unless they need them.
actions.done: Your contact has said yes and holds a paper list of your household, and they and a backup are written on the wallet cards and every Emergency numbers sheet and saved in each phone with ICE in front of the name.

actions.title: Ask your contact if they are willing, and explain the job
actions.why: A contact who does not know the role may ignore an unknown number or not know what to do with the message.
actions.how: Phone them and explain: after an emergency, each of us will text or call you to say we are safe and where we are, and we ask you to write it down and pass it on to the others. Ask them to save every household member's number under a clear name. Agree a second way to reach them, such as email or a messaging app, and check that their details on your cards are right.
actions.done: Your contact has said yes, has been asked to save everyone's number, and you have agreed a second way to reach each other.

actions.title: Give your contact a list of who is in your household
actions.why: Your contact can tell who is still missing only if they know whom to expect.
actions.how: Copy by hand, or photocopy, the names and mobile numbers from your Household sheet, and add your two meeting places and the address you would evacuate to. Leave off medical details unless your contact needs them. Post it or hand it over in person, and ask them to keep it where they can find it. This site sends nothing and only records that you did it.
actions.done: Your contact holds a paper list of your household's names and mobile numbers, your two meeting places and the address you would evacuate to.

actions.title: Give everyone a wallet card and save the number in each phone
actions.why: A phone can be lost, flat or locked, but a card in a wallet or school bag still gives the number.
actions.how: Print the Wallet contact cards sheet and cut out one card per person. Write by hand the out-of-area contact's name and numbers, two household mobiles and your meeting places; on a young child's card use the names they know, such as 'Grandma'. Put a card in every wallet, school bag and grab bag, and save the contact in each phone. The site only records that it is done.
actions.done: A filled-in wallet card is in every wallet, school bag and grab bag, and the out-of-area contact is saved in each phone.

actions.title: Run a leave-the-home drill from separate rooms
actions.why: People who have physically practiced an exit do it faster and with less panic than people who have only talked about it.
actions.how: Send each person to a different room. On a signal, such as a whistle or a phone alarm, everyone leaves by a planned exit and walks to the outside meeting place; time it from the signal to the last arrival. Move quickly but do not race, and bring children and pets as you would for real. Afterwards, talk about what slowed anyone down.
actions.done: Everyone has left from separate rooms and reached the outside meeting place, and you have the time from the signal to the last arrival.
actions.apartment: In an apartment the exits are your front door and the stairwells: use the stairs, not the elevator, and do not practice climbing out of windows above the ground floor.

actions.title: Repeat the drill from other rooms and by your second way out
actions.why: A real emergency may block your usual route, so the second route has to be as familiar as the first.
actions.how: Run the drill twice more from different rooms, one of them from bed in the dark using only the light you keep beside it. Use your second way out each time: the other stairwell in an apartment building, or a back door or ground-floor window in a house. Count the doors and landings on the way so that you could find the exit in the dark. Repeat the drill twice a year.
actions.done: You have run the drill twice more by your second way out, once from bed in the dark, and can say how many doors and landings you pass.
actions.apartment: Your second way out is the other stairwell; walk it all the way down and note where it comes out on the street.

actions.title: Practice Drop, Cover and Hold On
actions.why: Shaking gives you a second or two to act, and only a practiced movement happens that fast.
actions.how: On a signal, drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck with one arm, and crawl under a sturdy table or desk if one is within reach; if not, get beside an inside wall away from windows and tall furniture. Hold on to the table leg and stay there for a count of 60. Practice in each room you spend time in. In bed, stay there, turn face down and cover your head and neck with a pillow. With no table nearby, cover your head and neck with both arms. Do not run for a doorway, the stairs or the street. Do the drill with everyone at home.
actions.done: Everyone at home has dropped, covered and held on for a count of 60 in each room they spend time in.

region.label: Earthquake country
region.general: Where earthquakes are not a risk, practice the first minute of your area's most likely sudden hazard instead: for a tornado warning, go to the lowest inside room away from windows; for a fire alarm, check the door and follow your building's fire safety plan.

actions.apartment: In a tall building the swaying is stronger and lasts longer on high floors; stay inside and away from windows until it stops, and do not run for the stairs or the elevator. Once it has stopped fully, use the stairs, not the elevator.

actions.title: Work out the adapted move for anyone who cannot get under a table
actions.why: Someone who uses a wheelchair or walker, or who cannot get down and up again, needs their own practiced move.
actions.how: In a wheelchair: lock the wheels, bend forward as far as you can, and cover your head and neck with your arms, a pillow or a book until the shaking stops. With a walker or cane: sit on a chair, a bed or the walker's seat, then bend forward and cover your head and neck. If you cannot move: stay where you are and cover your head and neck with a pillow or your arms. Practice each person's version with them in the places where they spend most time.
actions.done: Each person who cannot get under a table has practiced their own version with you in the places where they spend most time.

region.label: Earthquake country
region.general: For each sudden hazard where you live, work out and practice the adapted first-minute action with every person who has limited mobility.

actions.cite_todo: The wheelchair and walker steps follow ShakeOut, which could not be opened; confirm them against an open official page on earthquake safety for people with disabilities.

actions.title: Join the Great ShakeOut drill in October
actions.why: A fixed date each year, shared with schools and workplaces, is the easiest way to make sure the practice actually happens.
actions.how: Put the third Thursday of October in your calendar. Register your household free at shakeout.org, and at the set time everyone does Drop, Cover and Hold On for one minute wherever they are. Use the same day to check your bags and replace anything out of date. In Oregon, the Great Camp-In asks households to live on their emergency supplies for a weekend; check the Oregon emergency management website for the date. After each drill, write down what you would change.
actions.done: The third Thursday of October is in your calendar, and your household is registered for the drill.
actions.apartment: For the Camp-In, camp indoors in one room instead of outside.

region.label: Earthquake country
region.general: ShakeOut runs in many countries; where earthquakes are not a risk, join your area's annual drill or hold your own lights-out evening on a fixed date each year.
